title: Tree Diameter
tagline: The longest path between any two nodes — found in a single post-order pass.

intuition.analogy: To find the two most distant rooms in a building, stand in each room and note the two longest hallways leading away from it. The longest such 'through path' over all rooms is the building's diameter.
paragraphs: The diameter is the longest path (counted in edges or nodes) between any two nodes. The key realisation: the longest path that passes through a particular node is the sum of the two deepest downward paths from that node.

So as you compute each node's height with a post-order DFS, you also combine its two tallest child heights to form a candidate 'through' path, and keep the global maximum. Heights flow up; the answer is a side effect.
For general (unrooted) trees there's also the elegant two-BFS trick: BFS from any node to find the farthest node u, then BFS from u to find the farthest node v; the distance u→v is the diameter.
intuition.keyIdea: The longest path through a node = its two largest child depths combined; track the max while computing heights.

steps.title: Post-order height
steps.detail: height(node) = 1 + max(height(left), height(right)); returns the longest downward path from this node.

steps.title: Combine the best two
steps.detail: At each node, candidate diameter = height(left) + height(right) (in edges). Update a global best.

steps.title: Return upward
steps.detail: Each call returns only its own height so the parent can use it; the diameter is accumulated globally.

codes.source:
def diameter(root):
    best = 0
    def height(node):
        nonlocal best
        if not node: return 0
        l = height(node.left)
        r = height(node.right)
        best = max(best, l + r)   # path through node (edges)
        return 1 + max(l, r)
    height(root)
    return best

complexity.timeReason: Single DFS visiting each node once.
complexity.spaceReason: Recursion stack proportional to tree height.

pitfalls: Confusing edge-count vs node-count diameter (off by one).
Returning the candidate path instead of the height from the recursion.
For unrooted/general trees, use the two-BFS method (only valid on trees, not graphs with cycles).

dryRun.clickMoment: At node 2 the two equal child heights combine into a length-2 path; at the root the deeper left subtree plus the right child give the true longest path. The maximum is captured exactly when DFS sits at the path's apex.

problems.title: Binary Tree Maximum Path Sum
problems.statement: Max path sum where a path is any node-to-node route.
problems.hint: Like diameter but with values; clamp negative child contributions to 0.

approach: Like diameter, but with values: the best path through a node is node.val + max(0,left gain) + max(0,right gain).
Each call returns the best downward gain a parent can extend (node.val + max child gain, clamped at 0). Track the global maximum path.

problems.title: Longest Univalue Path
problems.statement: Longest path where all nodes share the same value.
problems.hint: Extend a child's length only if its value matches.

approach: Same shape as diameter, but a child only contributes if its value equals the current node's value.
Each call returns the longest same-value arm downward; the answer is the largest left arm + right arm in edges.

problems.title: Tree Diameter (general tree)
problems.statement: Diameter of an undirected tree given as edges.
problems.hint: Two BFS passes: farthest from any node, then farthest from that.

approach: For a general (unrooted) tree, the diameter is found with two BFS/DFS sweeps: from any node find the farthest node u, then from u find the farthest node v.
The distance u→v is the diameter. Correctness follows because the farthest node from anywhere is always an endpoint of some longest path.

problems.title: Minimum Height Trees
problems.statement: Find roots that minimise tree height.
problems.hint: Peel leaves layer by layer; the last 1–2 nodes are the centroids.

approach: The roots that minimise height are the 1 or 2 centroids of the tree. Peel leaves layer by layer (topological trimming).
Repeatedly remove all current leaves; the last 1–2 nodes remaining are the answer.
